cultivar: Qi Lan (mostly Bai Ya Qi Lan from Pinghe, grown in Wuyi)
processing: Lighter oxidation than the heavy Wuyi cultivars and a light to medium charcoal roast, aimed at keeping the orchid aroma rather than building body.
harvest_season: One spring picking, late April to early May, as mature shoots with three or four open leaves.
appearance_dry: Slim, tight, dark olive-brown strips with a sweet orchid smell even before brewing.
appearance_wet: Medium-sized, soft olive-green leaves with thin red rims.
taste_profile: Orchid and sweet cream up front, honey and light roast behind, with a clean, short mineral finish and little bitterness.

brewing.notes: Boiling water, porcelain gaiwan to show the aroma. Slightly less leaf than for Rou Gui; it gives up its fragrance quickly and fades sooner, so enjoy the first five steeps.

vintage_note: Spring harvest of the current year, lightly roasted in early summer and often on sale by late summer, earlier than heavier yancha, with the year stated. Its light roast means it is best within a year or two of harvest and it is not a tea to age.
description:
Qi Lan, the rare orchid, is the friendly, fragrant end of Wuyi rock tea: a lightly roasted yancha whose whole personality is orchid aroma and soft sweetness. It is cheaper than the famous bushes and is many people's first Wuyi tea that did not taste of charcoal.

The name is confusing because it belongs to several cultivars. In the Wuyi Mountains most of what is sold as Qi Lan today is Bai Ya Qi Lan, the white-bud cultivar selected in Pinghe county in southern Fujian in the 1980s and planted in Wuyi from the 1990s, while a few older local Qi Lan strains also exist. Whatever the plant, the Wuyi version is made with the full yancha method: mature leaf, overnight shaking, strip rolling and a charcoal roast, just a lighter one than Rou Gui or Shui Xian get.

The light roast is deliberate. Qi Lan has a thin, aromatic leaf, and a heavy roast burns off exactly the part that makes it worth drinking. In the cup you get orchid and something like sweet cream in the first two steeps, then honey and toast, with a mineral finish that is clean but short. It does not have the thick body or the long cooling aftertaste of the older Wuyi cultivars, and it is wrong to expect them.

Brew it with boiling water in a gaiwan with slightly less leaf than a heavy rock tea and short steeps; it is a five-or-six-infusion tea rather than a ten-steep marathon. It is a good breakfast yancha and pairs easily with food.

It is sold by the current spring harvest and should be drunk fresh, within a year or two. Check that the seller names the year and whether the leaf grew inside the Wuyi scenic area, because much Qi Lan comes from outer-mountain plantings, and that is fine as long as it is priced that way. For the same aroma in a green, unroasted form, try Bai Ya Qi Lan from Pinghe itself.
sources_note: The identity of Wuyi Qi Lan with the Pinghe Bai Ya Qi Lan cultivar is the usual trade explanation; older local Qi Lan strains exist in Minnan and Wuyi and the labelling is not consistent.
